When K eats said "Beauty is truth, truth beauty " he came close to a prin c ipl e taught by the apostle Paul in his letter to the Galatians.

Paul assured the Galatians th at the Spirit and the flesh are opposed to each other, resulting in the Spirit-born man beingd eh cately balanced and divinely re strained. By himself a man cannot do the things he would. Spiritual coordination and poise come only from divine truth in action.

In every case, truth and beauty must exist first in the workman before they can bee videnc ed in his work. A true work of art is the projection of the artist; paint and canvas are only the vehicles of expression. Unless the artist has d eve loped akee n sense of beauty and balance in his own mind and spirit, he is not an artist. The canvas cannot portray what the man is not.

Jesus boldly claimed to be Truth and Life. The Bible teaches that allthings w ere made by Him, and without Him was not anything made th at was made. In Him allthings consist, or hold to gether. Our inability to grasp this amazing fact fully cannotd e tract from its force: that it is this same Christ in us whole nds beauty and balance to the total man. Our relationship to Christ does not involve religious acts only.

Christianity is the outflow of Christ through the total personality of anyone who bo ws to His Lords hip. Th eologi cal accuracy and religious forms are useless unless they are energized by Him who is the essence of Truth and Life. O ye re mphasis on activity without equal e m-phasis on communion and worship leaves us with the shell, without heart or passion.

Perhaps none of the arts illustrates this aspect of truth more pe rf ec tl y th an music. Just asa great painting is the express ion of a gre at artist, so good music. is the express ion of a great musician, whether hebe the com-pos er or the interpreter. The essential quality of the composition or the talent of the performer can be ex-pr eased only by exact timing and studied accuracy. The major and the minor, the dominant and the subordinate, the rest and the action must all blend toe xpr ess thebe auty of thew hole and the purpose of the musician.

Parallels in the spirit are quite obvious. Human nature must be s ubj ect to the divine. Truth and beauty of life will always result from thea bsolut e control of Him who is the Truth and the Life. It is not easy to accept this condition, however, because we are prone to think and act as though our lives are lived inseparate comp ar tm e nt s. We would relegate Christ to the church, theology to the study and business to the office with cl e ar-cut finality.
True Christianity cannot exist in a life thus dissected and compa rtm e nt ali zed. Christ cannot and will not exercise a partial Lord ship. The very thought is ridiculous and re pulsive.

The genius of Christianity is th at its trikes t hat balance between the flesh and the spirit which perm its Christ to be projected through all of the hum an personality. Paul expressed it beautifully, saying, “To me to live is Christ.” It is only to be ex p ec ted, for in stance, that the sci e nc es will ultimately clash with evangelical Christianity if they are viewed from the standpoint of human reason alone. They deal with only part of the truth. The s up e natural claims of Christ are based upon revelation. Reject rev elation and supe rn atura l in te rv mention in the affairs of man and your eject Christianity.

New Tes tame nt regeneration produces anew cr ea tur e rather than a new philo soph y. Anew philo soph y of life, however, results naturally from the new creation. Anew philosophy without the existence of a new cr ea tn re is impossible.

Again, it is both interesting and fright e nin g to study theme thods and means used to promote Christianity in our generation. Them ost charitable observer is forced to wonder at just what point our pro grams d epend upon God. The lack of true reverence and humility indicates the lack of divine consciousness.

Perhaps we may d ctc rmin e to some extent how seriously we are affected by this blight of rational iz ing the supernatural if we answer a few questions. To what extent in our service and worship arewed ominated by godly fear? Are our services marked by a profound r eve re nc e or by an obvious informality and m ark ct place familiarity? Is our life of personald evo tions motivated by a wholesome hunger and desire to experience the living Christ lest we walk in the flesh to our shame?

The Head of the church promised to be with us to thee nd of the age. He declared th at His church would be eh grace ri zed by s up e natural life and power. We cannot ask for more and we d are not accept less. If we are willing to subsist with a program of m ere orthodoxy we w ill be a prey for every c ult and extreme.
Beauty and truth are the Tes· ult of balance; and our true beauty is the beauty of the Lord H imse lf.-WrLLIAM F. BR YAN.

There has always been a contest between the supernatural and the natural. The bishop who recently declared that we should abandon all th at is supernatural in religion was only echoing some thousands of years later what the first family said in Eden. We usually expect, how ever, to find this sentiment outside the Christian church.

The clergyman in question judged himself when he said (in a sense boasted) that he belonged to the "once-born crowd." His are but the findings of a natural man. In fact, by his own admission he has no scientific right to declare himself on spiritual things. How can that which is of the earth, earthy, understand that which is of the heavens and spiritual?

The supernatural book the bishop so lightly dismisses, filled, he says, with myth and symbol, has already inerrantly ca talo gued him. The things of God are known only by the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:9-16).

I do not question the man 's right to his own religion, but let him be honest enough to admit it is not the religion of Biblical revelation. Surely a man should cease to be a Christian minister if what he believes and preaches is not Christianity. Christianity is supernatural or it is nothing. It claims to be supernatural in its origin, its precepts, its authority and final consummation.

When one examines this new theology he finds a thinly disguised conglomeration of naturalism, humanism, pantheism and existentialism. The God we are being offered is a nonpersonal "ultimate," " the essence of all being." We are told to look not up or out, but in. The more one knows of oneself the more one knows of God for God is to be found ultimately inbeing, and all be i~g is essentially God.

Such a concept sets aside the first three chapters of the Book of Romans. Sin imm e di lately loses its character. It is said to be m ere ly an aberration which "destroyed the harmony of affairs in the cosmics tate." It is no longer rebellion against a holy and right e on s God, something to be judged and punished and to be saved from. Rather it is only some thing to be ignored and daniel.

This obviates the necessity of an atonement for sin. In this new theology the literal incarnation of Christ is without meaning and, in fact, totally unnecessary. So it is " only a myth." All this leads to an inevitable conclusion. To deny a personal God, personal sin and a personal Saviour leaves man only with himself. He is his own god. But the Bibled declare that man 's nature is depraved; it says he has si un ed, th at there is not one who is righteous.

The gods men make, make men what they are. Our veneer of enlightened civilization may keep us from sprinkling chicken blood on a few stones and bent sticks on a jungle trail, but the naturalism of the man who does such makes it reasonable to him. Ours tells us something else, but the source and motivation are the same. Cain rejected the revealed way of sacrifice and salvation for a way that seemed right to him. Haman reasoned that the crystal waters of Damascus were to be pr cfc rr ed to the muddy Jordan. Certainly they appeared better, but they lacked what he needed most-h ea ling and cleansing. This is ever the way of man.

Does not this new theology ex plain the low state of m ora lity in what we call Christian nations? Man has sub st itut ed his religion for revealed truth. Each does what is right in his own sight. Th ere is no thought of God before his eyes day or night. Man in himself at one time became so vile and corrupted the world to such an extent that God had finally to send waters of judgment. Now again we are rushing toward judgment- judgment by fire.

What we have overlooked is that this whole philosophy is basically Antichrist: against Christ. Perhaps we have been so busy looking for a personal Antichrist, the Man of Sin, th at we have failed to recognize this fearsomed evelopme nt within the church it self.

Let us not think such a thing cannot happen among us who call ourselves evangelical. It is m ade to sound plausible, natural, reasonable. It beg ins with doubting-questioning-th e authority andine rranc y of the Scriptures: "Hath God said...?" "But did God really say that?" Even some cva ng eh ca ls are being caught in the current of this philosophy.

The apostle John told us nineteen hundred years ago th at many false prophets am gone out into the world. We are exhorted to try the spirits. "Every spirit that confesseth not that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is not of God: and this is th at spirit of antichrist " (1 John 4:3).

"Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God [ the second birth ].... Hereby know we that we dwell in him, and he in us, because he hath given us of his Spirit. And we have seen and do testify th at the Father sent the Son to be the Saviour of the world " (1 John 5:1; 4:13, 14).

What a glorious privilege to proclaim yet today th at at ra nscende nt God has made salvation possible by an act of grace. The s up e natural work of the Spirit of God transforms sinners into saints and pr e pares them for an eternity of personal fellowship with the God of creation and revelation. Any man may become a par taker by faith and obe di en ce. -NA THA N B AILEY.

Some believers consider sustained victory in Christian experience abnormal; others regard it asa sheer impossibility. Most of those who profess Christ's name accept habitual vacillation rather th an expecting continuous victory. Why is irr eg ularit y in one's Christian life condoned when in every other sphere it is condemned?

A watch owner expects d epen ability of his watch. A traveler expects trains to keep on schedule. Governments demand consistent airworthiness of all planes flown. We expect a pattern of good performance from our automobiles, even in a blinding blizzard in our rough Middle West winters. In thirty-below-zero weather motors may be hard to start, but finally they outride adverse conditions and " get up and go.“Likewise, after protracted sub-zero conditions,”dead" grass comes back to life.
If motors and nature can master a ppar en dy insurmountable obstacles, then surely God has resources available to His children whereby they too may be " more than conquerors."

Paul states categorically that we are more than conquerors: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?... Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us" (Rom. 8:35, 37).

"More than conquerors" in spiritual experience is not a chancy possibility ora nice poetic phrase. It is not in the past tense, nor is it dangled before us asa millennium luxury. There is no equivocation here. Thank God that by the finished work of Christ and the power of the in-dw telling Spirit we are to know continuous victory now.

This is not sinless perfection. Nowhere in the New Testament are we led to believe that in this life men can reach a state where they can not sin. Neither does the New Testament teach that we have to sin because in weak and wilted human nature th ere is an incurable spot that the blood cannot cleanse and that an omnipotent God can not cure. If the Christ of the cross, now risen and enthroned, cannot offer us victory over sin, we must capitulate to the sour song of J ean Paul Sartre: There's no way out of the human dilemma.

A critic says that our churches are full of empty people. He might be more correct if he said that they are half full of half-full p co pl e. The possibilities of grace have not been nor perhaps can be fully explored this side of eternity. But this much is sure: There are far too many limping Christians these days. Victory through Christ is not some thing we get five minutes after "we have shuffled off this mortal coil," as Shakespeare calls death.

Paul's more-than-conqueror cry is not the squeaking an immature and therefore unbalanced Christian. Paul is not exceeding the bounds of logic. Let us settle this in Christian expe ri ene e. In the context of Romans 8:35-37 this scar-marked warrior gives us the dimensions of this victory. He lists things external and things internal: tribulation, distress, p ers ecu tion, famine, n ake dn ess, peril, sword.

“Tribulation” is derived from a Latin word used to describe threshing. It refers to suffering the loss of all things and is external. But tribulation will rid us only of the chaff. Distress in the Greek connotation implies mental grief. Persecution covers every area of the human personality-body, mind and spirit. Famine, nakedness and sword obviously refer to the struggle that the body can know. Blessed be God that at this moment there are Christians who know and prove th at they can be what the Vulgate calls "over-overcomers."

When Daniel defiled the decree of Danus he was a conqueror; when he came out of the lion's den he was more thana conqueror. When the three Hebrew lad s, who would neither budge, bend nor burn, withstood Nebuchadnezzar they were victors. When they emerged smell-less from the furnace and caused the king to bless the Lord they were more than victors.

When asa sheep before her shearers is dumb our Lord curbed His power and refused to descend the cross, but submitted to a shameful mockingd eath, He was conqueror; when He rose again, triumphant over death, the grave and hell, He was more than conqueror.
Through Christ's over-overcoming, He offers us the almost uub eh cva hl e earthly bless ing of be ing joint heirs with Him in His triumph. The Book says that as He is, so are we in this world.

In the second century Blandina, a frail servant girl, was enveloped in a net and then tossed onto the horns of an angry bull. Lifted from this torment, she was next tortured for confessing "I am a Christian " by being set on are d-hot iron chair to die. There was never a murmur of grief or self-pity. Her very tormentors were tormented that their torment had failed. Blandina was more than conqueror: a victor-plus! Are we?-LEONARD

" If this completely new toothpick doesn't do more for you th an we claim, you may re turn it in ten days and we will gladly re fund your money." Sound familiar? Such ads make us aware th at the commercial world is anxious to give us an opportunity to try its products on a money-back-guarantee basis. We are today buying everything from hairpins to houses with the understanding that if we do not like them we can exchange them.

Whether we like it or not, we are be ing ca rn ed along on the strong tide of a tr y-it-and-see age. We choose the college we a tt end with the idea th at if we do not like it we can go to another. We select the major we study with the und erst an ding that we can reverse the order next semester. Unfortunately, this trial and error mentality does not end with things as insignificant as toothpicks or as important as college majors. Too often it is married into the realm of life vocations and even the choosing of a life partner. The results are devastating.

Nor have God 's p co pl e escaped this virus of chance in the choices they make. Was it a bent knee, an open Bible and the inward witness of the Spirit of God which led us to the church in which we now worship-or was it circumstances? Are we in our present occupation as the result of a glad c commit e nt to Christ, whatever His will might be, or are we just doing what seemed to be the opportune thing?

One finds it difficult to imagine Paul conceding that God had a plan for his life which could only be di s-covered through trial and error. With the apostle Paul, conversion, commitment, commission and communication were irr evoca hl ye twin ed. They were not separated experiences. They were the unfolding of one ex-p e ri ence of which conversion was the root. Paul's commitment to Christ was unqualified. He did not argue with the Saviour as to what his commission was to be, where it was to take him or how it was to be fulfilled. Commission follows hard on the heels of that kind of comm itm en t.

From the first Paul knew he was commissioned to communicate the gospel to the Gentiles. To this he earnestly gave himself, only to discover that geographic details were spelled out for him a step at a time. The apostle had no way to foresee that God 's path for hi1:1 would lead to such places as Ephesus, Philippi and Rome. He did not accept his commission on the basis that he could go to this city or that, or that he would receive this kind of response or that from his listeners. Suchd tails were not left toe ith er his whims or his abilities. The Lordship of Christ formed the foundation upon which the supe rstru c tur e of his service was built.

One finds it difficult to imagine Willing Carry ad-mitting a sense of obligation to pr each the gospel in India, but wanting to make sure by joining the British Army in India for a two- year stint. An open Bible, bent led Carry to the conviction that God wanted him in India. Trial and error had no place in the heart of this man who knew God was directing him to India.

It is a strange phenomenon that young people can graduate from our Bible institutes and Christian colleges today without the slightest concept of what God wants them to do. Even those few who have a leaning toward the foreign field do not feel prepared to move in that direction without first ta sting to see if it is good. This situation is so desperate th at some missions have found it necessary to arrange for eight een montl1s or two years of "s hort-t e rm " service so young people can find the will of God. Some Christian youth area ppar en dy join-in g the Peace Corps with the hope th at this will give them foreign field experience whereby they can ascertain whether they will fit into the missionary program or not.

All of this is a far cry from the plaint eaching of the Word of God concerning the discovery of God's will. A knowledge of the will of God is relative to one's desire to do the will of God. God does not reveal His will to those who are not gladly committed to it. A commission from God is relative to our commitment to God. Commitment is prerequisite to commission. There is no substitute for the bent knee, the surrendered h ear t, the open cove ring the will of God.

As this is being written the sixth immolation has taken place in Viet Nam. That men have the fortitude to burn themselves to death is an astonishing thing. While I do not wish to discuss the wisdom or merits of such acts, one cannot help but be moved to know that th ere are people who are so deeply committed to an ideal as to make the supreme sacrifice. The world stops to look, for our flaccid, easy age has become so accustomed to worship without sacrifice it is startled to find some persons whose devotion goes deeper.

The theme of this editorial, of course, does not refer to a sacrifice of atonement. That sacrifice was made once for all on Calvary. Our salvation depends upon the efficacy of that finished work, and by it we may draw near to God in worship. I am speaking, rather, of the sacrifice of devotion.

The gre ate st threat to our Christian faith and testimony is not external but internal. We need not fear at-ta ck from without; it is there duced faith within that is our weakness and shame. How can unmoved people move the world toward our Saviour? It is the cross in the heart that commends the cross of Calvary, but we have made the cross of Christ a raft upon which to drift to an easy heaven. Our dull unconcern, our deadly indifference, our serious disregard of obligation is a reproach to Christ. The Lord Himself declared, "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me."

It is not that we do not attend divine service, but that we approach God's altar with that which costs us nothing. We substitute sign and symbol for substance, but place and form can never suffice for sincerity and reality. It is not a question of this mountain or this church or even one ritual before another. The basis of our approach to God was written in the blood of Christ; in the face of this how dare we pl edge an anemic commitment! "W ere the whole realm of nature mine, I That were a present far too small; I Love so amazing, so divine, I Demands my soul, my life, my all."

The farther we depart from worship in spirit and in truth the more we turn to outward forms and ritual, to symbols and devices. These so-called aids to worship supplant the spontaneity of the Spirit and true heart devotion. In spite of congregational participation in such acts, we are in reality becoming spectator Christians. But there is no such thing as vicarious worship.

This is not to deny that th ere can be both beauty and meaning in such forms. Th ere are some who reach beyond them to reality and who in true spiritual understanding assign a depth of meaning to them. But there are many more who, lacking vital faith and spiritual discernment, derive satisfaction and think to please God merely through performing the act. Such are deceived.

It is significant that the men who have known God were often led away from the place of formal religious observances. Moses spent forty years in the desert. Paul was hidden three years in Arabia and th ere learned that true worship was a sacrifice of the heart. In the face of Calvary all the accouterments of which this Pharisee of the Pharisees so recently boasted became mockery.

Indeed Paul saw himself overwhelmingly in debt, an indebtedness that was twofold. The first was to his Lord and Saviour. Paul never ceased to marvel at the grace of God that had wrought salvation to him, the chief of sinners. From that moment he begin to offer the sacrifice of praise.

How can we take our salvation for granted? The greatest miracle of all is that I have been saved. Yet we stand week after week to sing dry-eyed of God's marvelous grace, and all too often what should be the highest devotion of our souls is offered more to the people than to our Lord. Instead of a message sung in a broken and tender spirit from a heart full of gratitude to God, we have an exhibition of human talent and achievement. It is an abomination in the house of the Lord.

But the apostle saw also that true he art worship in-volved him with his fellow men. Th ere is a sense in which we must fill up that which is be hind in the sufferings of Christ (Col. 1:24, cp. Matt. 20:22, 23). We can add nothing to the finished work of Calvary; that sacrifice was all-sufficient. But the spirit of Calvary ma y-and must-govern the Christian's life. Paul had much to boast of, but everything men count gain he cast away for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ. To him, to live was for Christ to live in him, he declared. Here pudiated pride of birth and position and a life of ease and unconcern. He knew that if he was to share in the redemption of the world he himself must bear the marks of Calvary, and he exhorted all believers to present themselves a living sacrifice unto God; m; 1ly in th is way could they demonstrate the perfect will of God. This life stands in stark contrast to the lust for place.

We live in a world of broken, bleeding men. Are we so intent upon the pursuit of our own pleasures and self-indulgences that our ears are stopped to their cry? Behold, see, ii> any sorrow like unto the sorrow of men who die of thirst when we have the water of life, of men who dwell in darkness while we have the light, who starve while we are satiated with the Bread of Life? " The gospel of a broken heart demands the ministry of bleeding hearts." God forbid that we dare to worship without sacrifice.-NATHAN BAILEY.

John F. Kennedy, thirty-fifth president of the United States, is dead. He was cut down by an assassin in the midst of what was apparently the spontaneous and enthusiastic tribute of the people of Texas, and the entire nation strives to find words to express the shock and shame of such an act. There is no politics in death, and where in expressing to Mrs. Kennedy, Caroline and John, our deep sympathy in their great sorrow. We trust that the entire Kennedy family may find access to the comfort that is found only in the abiding presence of God.
We pledge to Lyndon B. Johnson our loyal support as the head of our nation and assure him of our prayers in the awesome responsibility that rests upon him.

Two other lives were ended in the tragic events that begin November 22. One lost his life in the line of duty, apparently by the assassin of the president. The second man was killed, it was said, in order to avenge the life of the president.

The only explanation for all these actions is the depravity of the human heart, out of which comes rebellion against God and His law. The pride of man causes him to rebel against all authority, and he becomes a law unto himself, and both the judge and executor of that law. Basically this is anarchy, the sin of which Lucifer was guilty.

God has ordained that the peoples of earth are to dwell together in families of nations and are to come under governments. Romans 13 plainly states, "The pow ers that be are ordained of God. Whosoever therefore resisteth the power, resisteth the ordinance of God." Every person is exhorted to be subject unto the higher powers. As Christians we are confronted with certain fundamental principles as set forth in the Word of God. These have a direct bearing upon us as citizens of our state.

Our responsibility is at least threefold: First, there is to be submission to the government over us. The words of First Peter 2: 13 were written under one of the most despotic governments ever to exist, yet the exhortation is to be in submission to every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake. It is not a question of being in agreement with the ordinance, but rather of being in subjection to it.

Second, there is the obligation of support. When the people thought to trip Christ by the loaded question as to whether it was lawful to pay tribute to Caesar, He replied, "Render unto Caesar the things th at are Caesar's." This support may not always be financial, how ever. The police chief of one of the larg est cities in North America recently stated that the greatest problem for law enforcement agencies today is the apathy of the citizenry. A reflection of the moral state of the nation is seen in the fact that in the face of corruption and immorality of every description scarcely anyone is stirred to a sense of righteous indignation, and sothe wicked prosper. Very often the people deserve the government they get.

Our third responsibility is without a doubt the most important. Writing to Timothy, the apostle Paul exhorted that "first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men; for kings, and for all that are in authority; that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and honesty."

As long as it is in the world the church acts asa preservative. " Ye are the salt of the earth." Jeremiah the prophet reminded the people of his day that the whole land suffered because of the backsliding of God's people. God will not hold us guiltless for our lack of savour. We mourn the death of a president. Let us also mourn for our sins.-NATHAN BAILEY.

chapters.t: Willing Law on Heaven and Hell
p: As all temporary nature is nothing else but eternal nature wrought out of its kindled, disordered strife into a created or compacted distinction of its several parts, so it is plain that the whole of this world, in all its working parts, is nothing else but a mixture of heaven and hell. There cannot be the smallest things, or the smallest quality of anything in this world, but what is a quality of heaven or hell discovered under a temporal form....

0 man! consider thyself: here thou standest in the earnest, perpetual strife of good and evil; all nature is continually at work to bring about the great redemption; the whole creation is travailing in pain and laborious working, to be delivered from the vanity of time; and wilt thou be asleep? Everything thou hearest or seest says nothing, shows nothing to thee, but what either eternal light or eternal darkness hath wrought forth; for as day and night divide the whole of our time, so heaven and hell divide the whole of our thoughts, words and actions.

Stir which way thou wilt, do or design what thou wilt, thou must be an agent with the one or the other. Thou cast not stand still, because thou lives in the perpetual workings of temporal and eternal nature; if thou workest not with the good, the evil that is in nature carries thee along with it. Thou hast the height and depth of eternity in thee, and therefore be doing what thou wilt, either in the closet, the field, the shop or the church, thou art sow-ing that which grows and must be reaped in eternity....

Therefore awake, watch and pray and join with all thy force with that goodness of God which has created time and all things in it, to have a happy end in eternity. -From "An Appeal to All Who Doubt or Disbelieve the Gospel."
